strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: the reliability of model stitching as a proxy for functional similarity, building on recent critiques of TLM/DM in the literature.

The proposed FuLA method is well-motivated conceptually (Fig. 1) and technically simple to implement, extending the DM objective with function-consistent hints at deeper layers, connecting stitching to the knowledge-distillation literature in a novel way.

Extensive empirical investigation across three distinct testbeds (adversarial training, shortcut learning, cross-layer stitching) and multiple architectures (ResNet18, ResNet18 w/o residuals, ResNet34), with substantial supplementary results showing consistency of conclusions across architectures.

The paper convincingly demonstrates concrete failure modes of TLM/SLM (e.g., hallucinating robust accuracy at the cost of clean accuracy, exploiting shortcuts, overfitting to class subsets) via controlled, targeted experiments, which is a useful contribution to the field even independent of FuLA's own merits.
Reasonable engineering care is taken to disentangle confounds (e.g., re-implementing DM as a Hint with full training data and shared batch statistics to make comparisons fair).
weaknesses: Because no ground truth for functional similarity exists (acknowledged by the authors), essentially all evidence for FuLA's superiority is qualitative/visual (reading stitching plots), with no quantitative aggregate metrics, statistical tests, or confidence intervals to substantiate claims of increased 'reliability.'

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: FuLA is essentially FitNets-style hint-based layer matching applied to the stitching setup, extending the existing DM/Hint framing; the conceptual jump from prior functional-consistency KD work is small.

The paper's own experiments show FuLA is not immune to the pitfalls it critiques (e.g., still susceptible to shortcut exploitation in certain configurations, still exhibits directional asymmetry in cross-layer stitching), which somewhat undercuts the central claim that it is a decisively more reliable metric, though this is honestly reported.
No sensitivity analysis on the weighting scheme C in Eq. (5) (fixed to uniform) or on the choice of loss normalization, leaving open whether conclusions are robust to these design choices.

Presentation could be improved: dense notation, some typos ('swallower' for 'shallower', 'residual residual block'), and the stitching plots (the primary evidence) are visually dense and hard to parse quantitatively without accompanying summary statistics or tables.

The study is restricted to image classification with ResNet-family CNNs on CIFAR-10/small ImageNet subsets; generalization to other modalities, tasks, and larger-scale/transformer architectures is untested, limiting the demonstrated significance of the contribution.

The added computational cost of computing DM/FuLA hints over the full training set (versus the closed-form DM initialization) is acknowledged but not quantified, leaving practical scalability unclear.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and timely open problem: how to reliably evaluate functional similarity via model stitching, motivated by recent critiques of TLM/SLM (task-based) and DM (structure-based) settings.

The proposed FuLA objective is a reasonable and conceptually clean extension that connects the FitNets/knowledge-distillation "Hints" idea to the model-stitching literature, providing a task-agnostic alternative that also propagates functional information beyond the stitching point.

Experimental coverage is broad: adversarial training (robust/non-robust cross- and same-task), shortcut learning (pattern/location/ArUco), class-subset overfitting, and cross-layer/cross-architecture stitching, repeated across three architectures (ResNet18, ResNet18 w/o residuals, ResNet34) in the appendix, showing the qualitative trends are not cherry-picked to a single setup.

Implementation and training details (optimizer, hyperparameters, adversarial attack configuration, stitching-layer initialization) are documented thoroughly enough to support reproduction of the reported figures.

The paper offers some genuinely interesting qualitative observations (e.g., directional behavior persisting under a task-agnostic objective, penultimate-layer functional dissimilarity emerging under AT) that could stimulate follow-up work.
weaknesses: The central claim that FuLA is a "more reliable" functional similarity metric is essentially unfalsifiable given the explicitly acknowledged absence of ground truth; the entire evidentiary basis is qualitative visual inspection of many stitching-plot figures rather than any quantitative, statistically grounded comparison (no error bars over repeated runs/seeds, no aggregate summary statistic across settings, no significance testing), which weakens the soundness of the paper's strong reliability claims relative to its own stated limitation.

The core methodological contribution (adding FitNets-style layer-wise Hint losses on top of the DM objective, restricted to intermediate/pre-penultimate layers) is a fairly direct combination of two existing ideas (direct matching and function-consistent feature distillation, explicitly cited as prior work by Liu et al.), limiting the technical novelty of the contribution.

The weighting scheme for the multiple Hint terms (Eq. 5) is fixed to uniform by default with only a single follow-up ablation (Fig. 11) on cross-layer stitching; there is no systematic study of sensitivity to this hyperparameter or justification that uniform weighting is optimal or even a fair choice relative to the baselines.

Section 3.3 shows that FuLA still exhibits directional asymmetries in cross-layer stitching similar to TLM/DM, which somewhat undercuts the paper's narrative that task-agnostic alignment resolves the pathologies raised by prior critiques (Balogh & Jelasity); the paper reframes this as an "inherent property" without strong independent verification.

Figures are extremely dense (many small multi-panel plots per figure) and hard to parse quantitatively; the paper would benefit from tabulated numerical summaries (e.g., mean/variance of accuracy gaps, area-under-curve statistics) to substantiate claims currently made only through visual trend descriptions.

Scope is narrow: only image classification, only CNN/ResNet-family architectures, and only two datasets (CIFAR-10, a 10-class low-resolution ImageNet subset), which limits the generality of conclusions about FuLA's reliability across modalities and architectures.

No code/artifact release is mentioned, and given the complexity of the many stitching configurations (9x9 cross-layer grids, multiple shortcut types, multiple architectures), independent reproduction purely from the text/appendix would be labor-intensive.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: existing model-stitching optimality conditions (TLM/SLM) have been shown to be unreliable proxies for functional similarity, and the paper offers a concrete, principled alternative (FuLA) grounded in ideas from function-consistent knowledge distillation.

The proposed method is simple and elegant: it reuses the same affine transformation family used in prior stitching work but changes only the training objective to include latent 'hint' losses at layers downstream of the stitching point, while explicitly avoiding output-level (task) cues to reduce the risk of fabricated alignment.

The experimental design is thoughtful and multi-pronged: adversarial training (robust vs. non-robust), shortcut learning, and cross-layer stitching each probe a different failure mode (task overfitting, spurious cue exploitation, directionality), giving converging evidence rather than a single anecdotal result.

The authors identify and correct a confound in prior comparisons (DM was disadvantaged by using fewer training samples and not updating batch-norm running statistics) and re-implement DM as a fair 'Hint' baseline, showing good methodological care and self-awareness of prior work's potential pitfalls.

Extensive supplementary experiments across three architectures (ResNet18, ResNet18 w/o residual connections, ResNet34) and multiple shortcut types (pixel, ArUco, location) show that the qualitative conclusions are consistent, improving confidence in generality beyond a single architecture.
The related work section is thorough and clearly situates the contribution relative to model stitching, feature distillation, and function-consistency literatures.

The limitations section is honest, explicitly noting the lack of ground truth for functional similarity and the restriction to image classification, rather than overselling the method's definitiveness.
weaknesses: The central weakness, acknowledged by the authors themselves, is the absence of ground-truth functional similarity: all claims of FuLA's 'reliability' are inferred from qualitative visual trends in stitching plots and heatmaps rather than any quantitative, aggregatable metric of alignment quality or statistical test, making it hard to assess the strength/significance of the claimed advantage objectively.

The evaluation methodology relies heavily on visual inspection of many multi-panel line plots and heatmaps (e.g., Figs. 4, 5, 8, 10) with qualitative takeaways ('appears to,' 'suggests'); a numerical summary statistic (e.g., variance of clean/robust accuracy trade-off, deviation from expected interpolation) comparing methods would strengthen the evidentiary basis considerably.

The paper's own findings partially undercut the headline claim: even FuLA/Hint remain susceptible to shortcut exploitation in some configurations (Section 3.2), and cross-layer stitching still exhibits directionality under FuLA (Section 3.3), suggesting the proposed fix only partially resolves the identified reliability problems rather than solving them, which is understated in the abstract/introduction framing.

Scope is limited to CNN-based image classifiers (ResNet variants) on CIFAR-10 and a small low-resolution ImageNet subset; no experiments on transformer architectures, other modalities (e.g., language), or larger-scale settings, which limits confidence that the conclusions generalize.

The added computational cost of FuLA relative to DM/Hint (propagating through multiple downstream frozen layers per gradient step) is not quantified or discussed, despite being a practically relevant consideration for adoption.

The sensitivity of results to the hint-weighting scheme C is only lightly explored (Fig. 11, uniform weighting as default); a more systematic ablation over weighting choices would better support the design decision.

No code/artifact release is mentioned, and while appendix hyperparameters are reasonably detailed, full reproducibility (e.g., exact seeds, variance across runs, statistical significance of comparisons) is not established, since results appear to be single-run without error bars.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important critique of model stitching (Smith et al., 2025) that models relying on different information cues can appear functionally similar under standard forward-compatibility-only stitching, and proposes a well-motivated remedy grounded in the concept of identically represented inputs (IRIs).

The forward-backward compatibility framework is conceptually clean and provides a unifying lens across several stitching objectives (HLM, SLM, DM, and the newly proposed FuLA), clarifying how each formulation trades off supervision strength against susceptibility to shortcut/cue exploitation.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, VGG-16, ViT-Tiny, ViT-Base), datasets (CIFAR-10, LS-ImageNet-10, ImageNet-100), and stitching configurations (cross-seed, cross-supervision, cross-bias, cross-task, robust/non-robust), with consistent qualitative trends supporting the central claims.

Includes careful sanity checks (e.g., App. F.1 identical-model stitching with IRIs data) to validate that the constructed DIRIs_train dataset preserves semantic structure, strengthening confidence that observed effects are not artifacts of the IRIs generation procedure.

Revisits and meaningfully updates prior claims about robust vs. non-robust network similarity (Balogh & Jelasity, 2023), showing these are less functionally similar than previously reported once backward compatibility is accounted for, connecting the work productively to shared-invariance literature (Nanda et al., 2022; Feather et al., 2023).

The new FuLA objective is a reasonable middle-ground contribution bridging output-level and stitch-level matching, and the paper offers a useful comparison to CKA in the appendix showing added value of the invariance-aware functional framing over representational similarity.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution largely combines existing ingredients (model stitching machinery + IRIs from Nanda et al., 2022) rather than introducing a fundamentally new method; the main novelty is the reframing/operationalization (forward-backward compatibility) rather than a new algorithmic capability.

As acknowledged by the authors, there is no oracle notion of ground-truth functional similarity; validation relies on intuitive 'sanity checks' (e.g., expecting cross-bias models to be dissimilar) rather than quantitative or externally verifiable criteria, making it harder to assess whether invariance-aware stitching is truly more 'correct' versus simply more conservative.

IRIs generation on higher-resolution data (ImageNet-100) shows non-trivial semantic drift in the HLM sanity check (App. F.1), raising some concern about the fidelity of the DIRIs_train construction at scale, which is only partially addressed.

Some invariance-enabling formulations show unstable or degenerate behavior in specific configurations (e.g., SLM failing on ViT-Base identity stitching, SLM degeneracy under adversarial end models), and the paper does not fully resolve which formulation should be preferred, leaving the practical recommendation for users somewhat open-ended ('no clear winner').

The paper is limited to image classification tasks with relatively small-scale architectures/datasets; scalability of the optimization-based IRIs construction (200-step per-sample optimization) to larger models/datasets or other modalities is not discussed in terms of computational cost, which could hinder reproducibility/adoption.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and many objective variants (HLM, SLM, DM, FuLA) introduced somewhat abruptly; a clearer high-level summary table contrasting the formulations' properties (already partially given in the discussion) earlier in the paper would improve readability.

The comparison to prior invariance-aware representational metrics (Jones et al., 2022 with CKA) is relegated to the appendix and only lightly discussed, even though it seems central to positioning the paper's unique contribution relative to closely related work.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated critique of model stitching (Smith et al., 2025) by identifying that standard 'forward compatibility' stitching is blind to invariance properties, and proposes a conceptually clean 'forward-backward compatibility' requirement to address it.

Extensive empirical coverage: experiments span four architectures (ResNet-18, VGG-16, ViT-Tiny, ViT-Base), multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, LS-ImageNet-10, ImageNet-100), and four stitching objectives (HLM, SLM, DM, and the newly proposed FuLA), with results largely replicated in the appendix.

The revisited case studies (cross-bias/cross-task shortcut exploitation, robust vs. non-robust model stitching) produce intuitively sensible and interesting findings that materially revise prior conclusions in the literature (e.g., Balogh & Jelasity, 2023), suggesting genuine scientific value.

The paper includes a variety of sanity checks (App. F.1, connection to CKA in App. G) intended to validate that the IRIs-based dataset construction is faithful and that the invariance-aware framework provides information beyond existing representational similarity metrics.
The proposed FuLA objective is a reasonable, well-motivated middle ground between stitch-level and output-level matching, inspired by feature distillation literature.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims rest almost entirely on qualitative/visual 'sanity checks grounded on intuitive expectations' (explicitly stated in Sec. 3) rather than any quantitative or ground-truth notion of functional similarity; the paper's own limitations section admits the absence of an 'oracle' metric, which undermines confidence that the proposed method is more 'principled' rather than simply differently biased.

The IRIs-based dataset construction (DIRIs_train) is itself an approximate optimization procedure (200-step gradient descent from random noise) whose own sanity check (App. F.1) shows non-trivial semantic drift for ImageNet-100 under HLM, raising concerns about whether the reported effects for invariance-aware stitching are partly artifacts of this construction rather than genuine backward-incompatibility signals.

No formulation among HLM/SLM/DM/FuLA emerges as clearly reliable: SLM is shown to 'degenerate'/fail even on trivial identity-stitching sanity checks for ViT-Base (App. F.2), which is concerning given SLM is used as the sole output-level representative in the main robust/non-robust analysis (Sec. 3.3).

The paper explicitly concludes there is 'no clear winner' among invariance-enabling formulations and frames the result as a trade-off, leaving practitioners without actionable guidance on which stitching configuration to trust for a given problem, which somewhat limits the practical significance of the contribution.

Reproducibility is hampered by an incomplete/broken code repository link ('https://github.com/') in the submitted manuscript, and the IRIs generation procedure is computationally expensive (per front-model, per stitch-location optimization), which may limit adoption or independent verification.

The conceptual link between the simple 2D toy example in Fig. 1 (affine alignment of two 1D functions) and the deep, high-dimensional, non-linear stitching setting used in experiments is asserted rather than rigorously established, so the toy example serves mainly as an intuition pump rather than formal justification.

Presentation is dense with overlapping terminology (forward/backward/forward-backward compatibility, invariance-aware/invariance-enabling), and evaluating the many stitching-plot figures across architectures/datasets requires significant visual inspection rather than compact quantitative summaries (e.g., no aggregate statistics or significance testing across the many trajectories shown).

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely gap in the model-stitching literature: the paper directly engages with recent critiques (Smith et al., 2025) showing that standard forward-compatibility-only stitching can be misled by models relying on different information cues, and proposes a principled fix.

The core idea of combining identically represented inputs (IRIs) with model stitching to probe 'forward-backward compatibility' is a creative and technically sound synthesis of two previously separate lines of work (invariance probing via IRIs and functional similarity via stitching).

Extensive and systematic experimental design: results are validated across four architectures (ResNet-18, VGG-16, ViT-Tiny, ViT-Base), multiple datasets/resolutions (CIFAR-10, LS-ImageNet-10, ImageNet-100), and all major stitching objectives (HLM, SLM, DM, plus the newly proposed FuLA), lending good support to the generality of the claims.
The new FuLA objective is a reasonable and well-motivated addition that helps disentangle where functional misalignment arises (stitch-level vs. deeper latent levels vs. output level).

Careful methodological controls, including sanity checks that DIRIs_train does not semantically drift from Dtrain (App. F.1), controlling for initialization scheme and data augmentation effects, and multiple random seeds per configuration, which strengthens confidence that observed effects are due to the proposed mechanism rather than confounds.

The revisited analysis of robust vs. non-robust network stitching yields genuinely new and non-trivial conclusions that differ from prior literature, demonstrating the practical value of the proposed framework beyond merely replicating known failure modes.

Comparison to CKA (and an invariance-aware CKA variant) in the appendix helps contextualize the contribution relative to representational similarity metrics and shows the functional approach yields distinct, arguably more actionable, insights.
weaknesses: There is no ground-truth 'oracle' for functional similarity, a limitation the authors acknowledge; as a result many core claims rest on 'sanity checks grounded on intuitive expectations' (e.g., that cross-bias models 'should' be dissimilar) rather than on any independently verifiable notion of correctness, which somewhat weakens the strength of the central claims.

The forward-backward compatibility 'requirement' is stated fairly informally (representations processed 'in a similar manner'), without a precise, formulation-independent mathematical definition; its meaning is only made concrete through specific instantiations (HLM/SLM/DM/FuLA), which makes the general claim harder to evaluate on its own terms.

The IRIs generation procedure itself (200-step gradient optimization from random noise) introduces additional hyperparameters (step size, epsilon, tolerance ρ) whose sensitivity is not thoroughly ablated, and the validation of IRIs fidelity (App. F.1) is somewhat limited, particularly the noticeable divergence observed for ImageNet-100.

The paper reports no clear winner among the invariance-enabling formulations (Sec. 3.4), leaving practitioners without concrete guidance on which stitching objective to adopt, which limits the practical actionability of the framework despite its conceptual contribution.

Some sanity checks fail outright (e.g., SLM failing to recover the trivial identity transformation for ViT-Base in App. F.2) without a clear resolution or deeper investigation into why, raising some doubt about the robustness of SLM-based conclusions in that setting.

The presentation is dense, with a large combinatorial space of stitching objectives × standard/invariance-aware settings × architectures × datasets; while thorough, this can make it difficult for readers to extract clear, generalizable takeaways from the main text alone.
The term 'grounding' in the title suggests a stronger epistemic claim than what is actually delivered, given the explicitly acknowledged absence of an oracle notion of similarity.
